reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
clinicalPearls: A malignant epithelial tumour showing serous acinar differentiation, with cytoplasmic zymogen granules, most often arising in the parotid.
It is generally low-grade and is one of the commoner salivary malignancies of childhood and young adults, with a female predominance.
Occasional bilateral parotid involvement is described, an unusual feature among salivary malignancies.
Recurrent activation of the transcription factor NR4A3, through enhancer hijacking, is a characteristic molecular event and can be demonstrated by immunohistochemistry.
Tumour cells are typically DOG1 positive with an apical or membranous pattern, and the zymogen granules are periodic-acid-Schiff positive and diastase resistant.
Architectural patterns include solid, microcystic, follicular and papillary-cystic, the last of which can be misread as a benign cyst.
High-grade transformation (dedifferentiation) is the most important adverse event and markedly worsens the outlook.
Distinction from secretory carcinoma is essential; secretory carcinoma lacks true zymogen granules, is DOG1 negative and carries an ETV6 fusion.
reference.pathophysiology: Acinic cell carcinoma arises from cells committed to serous acinar differentiation, recapitulating the zymogen-granule-producing acinar cells of normal salivary tissue. A recurrent structural rearrangement repositions a strong enhancer adjacent to the NR4A3 gene, driving marked overexpression of this nuclear receptor transcription factor and promoting tumour cell proliferation. The neoplastic cells retain the capacity to synthesise serous secretory (zymogen) granules, which underlies both the histological appearance and the periodic-acid-Schiff staining, and they are arranged in solid, microcystic, follicular or papillary-cystic patterns. Although most tumours behave in a low-grade fashion, a subset undergoes high-grade transformation with loss of acinar differentiation, increased mitotic activity, necrosis and a greatly increased propensity for nodal and distant spread.
additionalInvestigations: Fine-needle aspiration cytology, recognising its known limitations for this tumour
Core or excisional biopsy for definitive histology
Molecular testing for NR4A3, and for ETV6 to exclude secretory carcinoma
MRI of the primary and ultrasound or CT of the neck for staging
Cross-sectional or functional imaging where high-grade transformation is suspected
redFlags: Features of high-grade transformation such as necrosis, marked pleomorphism and high mitotic count
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable for conventional low-grade tumours managed with complete excision. High-grade transformation substantially worsens survival, and late local recurrence or metastasis can occur, so prolonged follow-up is advised.
pitfalls: Misclassifying secretory carcinoma as acinic cell carcinoma and missing a targetable fusion
Underestimating or failing to sample areas of high-grade transformation
Mistaking a low-grade tumour for benign or normal acinar tissue on cytology
Achieving inadequate surgical margins because of an infiltrative edge
references: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
Gnepp's Diagnostic Surgical Pathology of the Head and Neck
Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
management: Complete surgical excision as the mainstay, typically parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve where oncologically feasible
Neck dissection for clinically or radiologically involved nodes or in high-grade disease
Adjuvant radiotherapy for high-grade transformation, incomplete resection, positive margins or other adverse features
Prolonged clinical and imaging surveillance given the risk of late local recurrence and metastasis
Consider systemic therapy or clinical-trial enrolment for unresectable, recurrent or metastatic disease, recognising its limited chemosensitivity
Multidisciplinary head-and-neck team management spanning surgery, pathology and oncology
